prompt.context: This is a game show style case with three independent mental math and logic puzzles. No paper is permitted for the first question.
prompt.question: Solve the following three problems: (1) What is 78 times 82? No paper permitted. (2) How many handshakes will eight people have to exchange when they are all leaving the room? (3) You have a board of 64 squares of equal size (8 squares by 8 squares). You eliminate two of the board's corners that are diagonally opposed to one another. You are given a limitless number of dominos, each composed of two squares (same size as those of the board). Can you fill the board with dominos so that each remaining square is covered? You may not juxtapose dominos.

framework: Recognize each puzzle as an independent problem requiring a distinct reasoning approach
Q1: Apply algebraic identity (difference of squares) to simplify mental arithmetic
Q2: Apply combinatorics / triangular number logic to count unique handshake pairs
Q3: Apply parity / coloring argument (chessboard logic) to prove impossibility

questions.guidance: A strong answer quickly approximates (~6,400) then applies the difference-of-squares identity to get the exact answer. Recognizing 78 = 80-2 and 82 = 80+2 is key.

questions.prompt: How many handshakes will eight people have to exchange when they are all leaving the room?
questions.guidance: A strong answer recognizes that each person shakes hands with every other person exactly once and sums the decreasing series: 7+6+5+4+3+2+1.

math.setup: Person 1 shakes 7 hands, Person 2 shakes 6 (new) hands, ..., Person 7 shakes 1 hand

questions.prompt: Can you fill the mutilated 8×8 board (two diagonally opposite corners removed) with dominoes?
questions.guidance: A strong answer uses a coloring/parity argument. Think of the board as a chessboard. Each domino must cover exactly one black and one white square. Two diagonally opposite corners share the same color, so removing them leaves an unequal number of black and white squares, making tiling impossible.

math.setup: Standard chessboard has 32 black and 32 white squares. Two diagonally opposite corners are the same color.
steps: Removing both same-color corners leaves 30 of one color and 32 of the other (62 squares total)
Each domino covers exactly 1 black + 1 white square
With unequal counts of black and white squares, complete tiling is impossible
math.answer: No — the board cannot be filled.

recommendation: Q3: No — the board cannot be tiled; the coloring argument proves it is impossible
risks: Rounding error if candidate only approximates Q1 without seeking exact answer
Double-counting handshakes (each pair counted twice) in Q2
Attempting trial-and-error on Q3 without recognizing the structural impossibility
